entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Pompeius Senecio Sosius Priscus, a prominent Roman senator of the late 2nd century CE, ascended to the consulship in 169 CE, during the tumultuous reign of Emperor Marcus Aurelius. His extensive full name, comprising an unparalleled 38 elements, stands as the longest attested for any individual in ancient Rome, a testament to the complex adoption and inheritance practices among the Roman elite. Born into a distinguished senatorial family with roots in Lucania, his career exemplifies the enduring power of aristocratic networks and the intricate mechanisms of social advancement within the Antonine dynasty, where familial prestige often dictated political trajectory.

Priscus's career trajectory saw him serve as *legatus Augusti pro praetore* (imperial legate) of the province of Lycia et Pamphylia, an important administrative and military post, before reaching the apex of the Roman political system as *consul ordinarius*. This prestigious appointment placed him at the heart of imperial governance, making him one of the two eponymous magistrates for that year, a critical period marked by the Marcomannic Wars and the burgeoning challenges to Roman stability. His administrative experience in various provinces, though not exhaustively documented, would have contributed to the operational efficiency of the vast Roman Empire.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Quintus Pompeius Senecio Sosius Priscus held one of the highest offices in the Roman Empire, the consulship, during a pivotal period. His extraordinarily long name provides unique, detailed insights into Roman elite social structures and onomastic practices, becoming a key data point for understanding ancient Roman identity.
